rv.q: "The Drowsy Chaperone" is so stupid it's smart.
Theo Ubique’s joyous revival of the Tony-winning musical turned this critic into a tap-dancing, high-kicking fool.
This play is simply a joy and Theo is always an unforgettable experience.
THE DROWSY CHAPERONE is the quintessential show for a delightful evening in the theatre.
It's goofy and quick and becomes a paean to the theatre, to living life as fully as we can, and to the joy of performing for all these young people who cannot stop smiling the entire time.
There really isn't a weak link here, including the four-piece band led by music director Eugene Dizon.
If ever a play was designed to lift the spirit and take our minds off the cares of the world, The Drowsy Chaperone may be just what is needed.
From start to finish, it was clear that the actors were having fun, and their joy was certainly contagious.
The result is a confection of a songbook, evocative of both Jazz Age and late 20th-century productions, somewhat bittersweet, but mostly fluffy, energetic and fun.
Escape is a balm, and this show is a dose of happiness we all may need.

Theo’s signature touch—immersive staging and emotional honesty in its by-design close quarters—elevates the show well beyond simple parody; it’s a more moving and meaningful tribute to musical theatre that leaves you smiling long after the final note.
Full of non-stop jokes that have the audience laughing the entire show, The Drowsy Chaperone is a good fit for all theatre lovers and non-theatre lovers alike.

cn.t: Critics embrace this joyful production as delightful escapist entertainment, praising Steve McDonagh's narration and Theo Ubique's intimate staging. The affectionate Broadway satire delivers non-stop laughs and captures the show's love letter to musical theatre.
